guide.intro: Plan to the end of January, started Fri 13 Nov 2026. Weeks 1–6: DP in depth — 60 problems, two new a day — with two concept-touch problems a day (a graph problem every day for the first four weeks) and daily blind-primitive drills. Weeks 7–11: every other topic, one family a week — 75 named problems on the clock, 15 mocks, with interview scenarios and Googleyness on alternate days. Shaped by the Google process as reported in November 2026.

research.title: Checked 11 Nov 2026 — how solid this is
research.text: Nothing below comes from a Google-published page. It rests on six first-hand LeetCode Discuss reports from India L3/L4 loops in 2026, plus Google statements relayed by the press. Treat the shape as reliable and the details as reported; confirm your own loop with the recruiter.

research.title: India L3/L4 is now a 2+2 loop
research.text: Recruiter call → GHA (sometimes a coding OA) → two virtual, eliminatory rounds (one DSA, one Googleyness) → two in-person DSA rounds back to back on one day at the Bangalore or Hyderabad office → team matching → hiring committee → offer. Four interviews, three of them DSA, no system design round at L3 or L4. With only four rounds, one weak round is hard to absorb.

research.title: The gates before any interview
research.text: The GHA is a ~30-minute work-style questionnaire with a reported six-month cooldown on failure. Some India L4 lateral candidates in 2026 also got a webcam-proctored coding OA: two questions in about 60 minutes, one of them a hard DP. A failed interview loop reportedly costs 12 months.

research.title: Final rounds are face to face
research.text: Google brought back in-person rounds to counter AI cheating; in India the two final DSA rounds are in person. Whether that means a whiteboard, a provided laptop or a shared doc is not established — ask. Practise without an IDE, autocomplete or a run button, talking aloud.

research.title: What the coding rounds ask
research.text: One problem per 45-minute round plus one or two follow-ups (generalise a constraint, N-ary, negative weights, minimise API calls). Mostly story-wrapped variations of known patterns, not verbatim LeetCode. In about 17 reported 2026 problems: graphs ~5 (BFS, Dijkstra variants, minimax path), arrays / prefix sums / hashing / Kadane ~5, strings ~3, then tree DP, greedy / heap, sliding window, an interactive binary search and a probability puzzle. Classic 2D DP is rare live but showed up in the OA. Speed is graded: candidates who solved everything were still marked down for pace.

research.title: Googleyness is early and eliminatory
research.text: One 45-minute virtual round before the onsite, at both L3 and L4: roughly 8–10 rapid behavioural questions with cross-questioning (ambiguity, negative feedback, conflict, missed deadlines, credit). New in 2026: questions about how you use AI in daily work. Have 7–8 STAR stories and a concrete AI answer.

research.title: AI in the interview
research.text: Standard coding rounds remain AI-prohibited. Google confirmed in May 2026 a pilot of a code-comprehension round — read, debug and optimise an existing codebase with Gemini as the only approved assistant — for junior and mid-level engineers on select US teams, and said in October 2026 that it is still piloting changes and that AI fluency is expected of all software engineers. No India L3/L4 report of that round was found as of November 2026.

research.title: Hiring climate
research.text: Alphabet headcount was about 204,800 at the end of September 2026, up about 7.7% in a year; 2026 layoffs found were small and team-level. India is actively interviewing at L3 and L4. Expect friction, not a freeze: reschedules, recruiter changes, and team matching (which in India can come before the hiring committee) taking from two days to about five weeks.

research.title: Google problems come wrapped in ambiguity
research.text: The most consistent 2025–2026 theme isn't difficulty — it's deliberately vague framing. "Parse a chat log and return the K most talkative users", "a network of teleporters, some broken, return the path". Underneath: top-K heap, BFS, DP. The algorithm is standard; the statement is not. Nobody practises this, and it's why strong LeetCode solvers fail Google specifically.

rules: Weeks 1–6: new learning is DP only. Two problems a day, done properly, beats four done shallowly.
Before any DP code: state (dp[i] = precise English meaning) · transition · base · order, written down.
No editorial before 25 minutes. Not a hint, not a tag, not an LLM.
Every DP problem is re-solved at +3 and +14 days, from a blank file. This converts exposure into retrieval. A re-solve that lands on the contest or rest day moves to the next working day.
After the editorial: close it, re-implement from scratch.
Concept-touch problems are for staying in contact with a topic, not for mastering it again: 25 minutes each, then stop. They are not re-queued.
20% of all practice happens in a blank Google Doc or on paper. No IDE, no autocomplete, no execution.

dailyTemplate.content: 2 new DP problems. Four lines first (state · transition · base · order). 25-min hard timer → 5 min writing what you know and which constraint you haven't used → editorial → close → re-implement blank.
The day's +3 and +14 queue, 12-minute timebox each. Even on bad days. Short on time? Cut Block A, never Block B.

The day's 2 touch problems: one from trees / graphs / backtracking, one from strings, arrays, binary search, heaps, linked lists or design. 25 minutes each. Missed the pattern → read the editorial and add one trigger line in Notes.

The weekday's five blind primitives (22 to 25 min, on a stopwatch), each from a different topic: the Drills tab shows the day's five. Every primitive comes up once a week, none twice. Each checked on its test problem. Plus the weekday extra: Tue debug hunt · Wed code quality · Thu ambiguity drill · Fri code comprehension · Sat cold-combo (weeks 1–6).

dailyNotes: Weekly shape: 5 working days (Fri, Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu) + contest on Saturday + rest on Sunday. Week 1 starts on a Friday, so every plan week runs Friday to Thursday.
Contest day (3h): 90-min LeetCode weekly or biweekly, 90-min post-mortem solving everything missed, untimed. Then stop.

Touch block: a graph problem every working day in weeks 1–4 (union-find and Dijkstra first — that week was never re-solved), plus one from the rotation trees · strings · prefix/stack/intervals · binary search · heaps · backtracking · linked lists/design.

Weeks 7–11 take one topic family a week (strings · arrays · binary search and heaps · linked lists, design and bits · graphs, trees and backtracking). Every problem, scenario, mock and story is named on its day. Scenario and Googleyness alternate days.

phase2Template.content: The day's 3 named problems from the week's topic, 35 minutes each on a hard clock, spoken aloud, brute force first, one follow-up variant each. Mon and Wed on paper or a whiteboard.

Alternate days. C: the day's scenario from a 2026 Google report, posed vaguely — specification in ≤5 minutes of questions, then solve. G: the day's Googleyness task (stories written in weeks 7–8, rehearsed in week 9, mock rounds in weeks 10–11).
The day's five blind primitives every working day, as on the Drills board (22 to 25 min). On Fri, Tue and Thu add the mock interview on the named problem (45 min), unopened until the clock starts.

drills.name: Spaced re-solve
drills.text: 12-minute timebox. Can't finish → failure → re-queue +3/+14 from today. Clean pass at +14 → retire. Failed twice → add +30. Passing means you reconstructed the reasoning, not recalled the code — typed something memorised and can't state the invariant out loud? Fail, even if it submits green.

drills.name: Ambiguity drill
drills.text: Take a solved problem and rewrite it as a vague real-world scenario the way a Google interviewer would pose it. Come back to it a week later (or have a friend read it cold) and practise the derivation out loud: clarifying questions, stated assumptions, explicit edge cases. Source scenarios from Discuss Google interview-experience posts.

drills.name: Variant generation
drills.text: After solving anything, pick one variant and solve it. Reported Google rounds routinely include 2–3 follow-ups after the initial solve — this drill is the second half of every round.

drills.name: Triage
drills.text: Ten problems you will not solve, 90 seconds each: constraints suggest · trigger phrase · pattern guess · why not greedy. Then check tags. Ten pattern-recognition reps at a tenth the cost of solving ten.

drills.name: Blind primitives
drills.when: Daily · about 25 min · five topics a day · stopwatch
drills.text: Five primitives a day, each from a different topic, the same every week. Binary search, windows, trees, graphs, DP and stacks all come up on two or three separate days, so no topic goes a week untouched, and no primitive appears twice in a week. The DP primitives are on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. Instantiate, don't stub. Time every attempt with a stopwatch and log the real number: a rounded guess makes the at-target badge meaningless. Verify every attempt by submitting it to the test problem listed under the primitive. KMP (Monday), Fenwick tree (Wednesday) and segment tree (Friday) are on the board as optional extras: do them after the day’s five. The five primitives take 22 to 25 minutes; the weekday extra (Tuesday to Friday) adds 20 to 30 on top. When the day runs short, cut the weekday extra first, never a re-solve.

drills.name: Debug hunt
drills.text: Break a solved problem deliberately (off-by-one, flipped comparison, missing base case, answer recorded before the shrink). Wait a day. Find it by hand-tracing a small input — no execution. Exactly what a shared-doc round demands.

drills.name: Code quality pass
drills.text: Rewrite two of the week’s solutions as if for code review: descriptive names, extracted helpers, guard clauses, no magic numbers. Could an interviewer follow this while you narrate? Google grades readability explicitly.

drills.name: Code comprehension
drills.text: Open an unfamiliar 200–500 line file from a real open-source repo, ideally a language you don't write daily. Out loud: what does it do in two sentences · inputs, outputs, invariants · where would a bug hide · complexity of the hot path · what would you change. This is the pilot round's exact shape.

drills.name: Cold-combo
drills.text: Write a primitive inside an actual problem under time pressure, rather than in isolation. The check against a skeleton becoming its own memorised artifact. Stops after week 6: from week 7 the three timed problems a day and the mocks do the same job.

guide.bugLog: Every failed primitive attempt gets one line, e.g. "Dijkstra — forgot to skip stale PQ entries on pop". This selects your first two primitives each day; after a month it maps your personal bug fingerprint. Keep it in Notes.

guide.primitivesGoal: Blank file, zero reference, timed. The 25 primitives are split five a day, each from a different topic, so every primitive comes up once a week and every topic two or three times. Targets are fluency targets, not learning targets. Each primitive lists a test problem: paste what you wrote and submit it, so correctness is checked by a judge and not by eye.

verbalProtocol: Restate the problem in your own words. Confirm.

Ask 2–3 clarifying questions and state your assumptions explicitly — with Google's ambiguous framing this is scored. Input size? Duplicates? Ties? Who parses the input? Fits in memory? Return the value or the actual path?
State a brute force and its complexity. Skipping this reads as pattern-matching.
Propose the optimisation and its complexity before coding.
Code, narrating. Clean names — readability is graded.
Dry-run a small example by hand, out loud. No execution available.
Volunteer your own test cases — interviewers ask candidates to enumerate test scenarios unprompted.
State time and space complexity, justified. Offer a follow-up improvement.
googleyness: Disagreeing with a senior engineer's technical decision (reported 2026 prompt)
A project you drove without authority
exitCriteria: New DP problem: state / transition / base / order correct before any code.
Unseen DP medium: pattern in ≤5 min, solved in ≤25, bug-free first submission, ~80% of the time.
Unseen DP hard: solved in 40–45 min about half the time.
Two follow-up variants handled on the spot without restarting (reconstruct the answer, count instead of optimise, tighten the space).
From memory in under 8 min: knapsack table · LIS O(n log n) with reconstruction · edit distance grid · bitmask DP over subsets.
Every primitive at its target time, verified on its test problem.
Time and space stated and justified unprompted, every time.
Unseen medium on any topic: pattern in ≤5 min, solved in ≤25, about 80% of the time. Ambiguous scenario → correct specification in ≤5 min of questions.
Fifteen mocks done and scored, at least two with another person and two on paper or a whiteboard.
Eight Googleyness stories written and rehearsed, plus a concrete answer on how you use AI at work; GHA positions written.
failureModes: Coding before the four lines are written. Most DP failures are a wrong state, not a wrong loop.
Skipping Block B. Revision feels unproductive because you're re-solving things you "already know." You don't — in September and October 96 of 158 scheduled re-solves were skipped.
Letting the touch block grow. It is 25 minutes a problem to stay in contact, not a second curriculum.
Logging drills in batches. One day of 18 drills is not 18 days of 1.
Skipping variants. At Google that's skipping half of every round.
Jumping straight to optimal. Reads as memorisation. State the brute force.
Only practising in an IDE. Shared doc, no autocomplete, no execution — and in-person rounds mean paper too.
Skipping the rest day. A burnout crash costs two weeks you don't have.
recruiter: Is my loop the 2+2 format: virtual DSA + virtual Googleyness, then two in-person DSA rounds?
In the in-person rounds, do I write on a whiteboard, a provided laptop or a shared doc?
Will I get a coding OA before the screen, and on which platform?
Does my loop include the Gemini-assisted code-comprehension round? If yes, weight the Friday drill heavily.
Is AI permitted in any round? Assume banned unless you have it in writing.
Can I have two to three weeks between the virtual rounds and the onsite? Candidates report this is granted on request.

notes: Burst Balloons was reported verbatim in an L4 onsite — the candidate solved it, missed an edge case, then handled three follow-ups.

Burst Balloons is the classic interval-DP trap: bursting first doesn't decompose, bursting last does. Sit with why until it clicks. Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick is the same idea with the cut made first.
Partition DP shape: dp[i] = best over the last piece ending at i. With a limit on the number of pieces it becomes dp[i][k].
Split Array Largest Sum has two solutions. The DP is O(n²k); binary search on the answer is O(n log sum). Know both and say when each applies.

notes: Tree DP is the post-order aggregate from the tree weeks: return a tuple upward, combine at the node. Sum of Distances in Tree is rerooting: one post-order pass for subtree answers, one pre-order pass to move the root.

Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix is DP on a DAG — the same memoised DFS as the graph weeks. Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling: sort by end time, dp[i] = max(skip, profit + dp[last job ending before this one starts]), found by binary search.
Bitmask DP trigger: n ≤ 20 and the state is "which items are used". dp[mask] or dp[mask][last]. Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes is BFS over (node, mask).
Game DP: dp = best score difference the player to move can force. Frog Jump is a state-design problem: the difficulty is deciding what the state is, not the transition.
Left out on purpose: digit DP, probability DP and the rarest hards. They almost never decide a Google round; the two weeks they would cost go to mocks.

notes: No new DP from here. Weeks 7–11 take one topic family a week, three named problems a day, all on a 35-minute clock, spoken aloud. Mondays and Wednesdays are on paper or a whiteboard: no editor, no run button.
The scenario block (C) and Googleyness (G) alternate days. Mock days are Thursday, Monday and Wednesday: do not open the mock problem before the 45-minute clock starts.

One sliding-window template: expand right, shrink while invalid, record after the shrink. "Exactly k" is atMost(k) − atMost(k−1). Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K breaks the template because of negatives: it needs a monotonic deque over prefix sums.
Text Justification and atoi are pure edge-case problems — exactly the careful boundary handling Google grades.
